name.english: Banana Rhizome in Ghee and Spices

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Kanda-saka (rhizome vegetables) section

steps: Cut the banana rhizome into pieces.
Boil the pieces in water until tender.
Cook in ghee together with asafoetida, rock salt and black pepper.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold, delicious, appetiser, strength-promoting, beneficial for hair, digestive stimulant; cures burning sensation and acidity.

notes: Rhizome (kanda) preparation. Modern equivalent of the corm is plantain/banana stem base.

name.english: Elephant Foot Yam in Sesame Oil

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Kanda-saka (rhizome vegetables) section

steps: Boil the yam pieces in tamarind-leaf decoction or sour gruel to remove acridity.
Cook in sesame oil with turmeric juice, asafoetida water, salt, fragrant spices and black pepper.

properties.ayurvedic: Stimulates digestion; light and un-unctuous; cures piles and kasa (cough).

notes: Elephant foot yam must be boiled in a sour medium first to cut its natural acridity — a step still followed today.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Vrintaka preparation 10

steps: Roast the brinjals directly on charcoal.
Crush the roasted flesh and mix in ghee.
Add rock salt.
Bake (finish) on a low fire.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetite stimulant.

notes: The text itself notes this is 'the very popular preparation known as Bengana Bhartha nowadays' — a documented historical ancestor of modern baingan bharta.

name.english: Steamed Brinjal in Ghee and Spices

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Vrintaka preparation 1

steps: Cut the brinjals with their foot-stalks.
Steam them in sour liquid.
Cook in ghee with coriander seeds, wet ginger, turmeric, salt and black pepper.
Add fried asafoetida.

properties.ayurvedic: Digestive stimulant.

notes: One of thirteen documented brinjal preparations in the Kshemakutuhalam.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Bimbaphala preparation 1

steps: Fry the pieces of ivy gourd in a small amount of ghee with asafoetida.
Add rock salt and black pepper.
Cook until done.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetite stimulant. (The gourd itself is cold; per Caraka Samhita it alleviates kapha and pitta.)

notes: Modern tindora/ivy gourd stir-fry closely mirrors this method.

name.english: Sweet Ash Gourd in Milk and Ghee

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Kusmanda preparation 3

steps: Boil the ash gourd pieces in milk.
Crush them.
Cook in ghee.
Add sugar.
Sprinkle sweet-smelling powders such as cardamom and black pepper.

properties.ayurvedic: Ash gourd is nourishing and cold; cures raktapitta (bleeding disorders).

notes: An early milk-and-ghee sweet, conceptually close to modern petha / ash-gourd halwa.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Karavelli preparation 2

steps: Cook the bitter gourd in a large amount of oil with asafoetida.
Add black pepper and rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Purgative, light, cold, bitter in taste; cures raktapitta, jaundice, anaemia, kapha, obesity and worms.

notes: A second Kshemakutuhalam method boils the karela in buttermilk first, then cooks it in fresh butter with rock salt.

name.english: Banana Cooked in Ghee and Spices

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Kadaliphala

steps: Peel the bananas and cut into pieces.
Cook in ghee with asafoetida.
Add rock salt, cardamom and black pepper.

properties.ayurvedic: Sweet, cold, wind-forming, unctuous and heavy; alleviates pitta; cures burning sensation and vata diseases.

notes: Uses firm/raw plantain rather than ripe dessert banana, given the savoury spicing.

name.english: Cucumber Simmered in Milk with Cardamom

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Karkati preparation 2

steps: Boil the cucumber in milk.
Cook in ghee with black pepper, sugar and cardamom.

properties.ayurvedic: Exceedingly appetising; cold, un-unctuous, constipative, heavy and sweet in taste.

notes: Uses the large mature cooking cucumber (dosakaya-type), not the small salad cucumber.

name.english: Roasted Indian Gooseberry with Ghee and Cumin

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Amalaka

steps: Roast the gooseberries on fire and crush them.
Add ghee, cumin seeds and salt.
Fumigate with the smoke of asafoetida.

properties.ayurvedic: Digestive stimulant, rejuvenating (rasayana) and wholesome; alleviates all three doshas; cures raktapitta and fever.

notes: Asafoetida-smoke fumigation (dhupana) is an authentic historical flavouring technique.

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, Bhartur Upabhogakarana (food/enjoyment section) — fish preparation

steps: Cut the fish into pieces and wash them well.
Cook the pieces with Malabar tamarind (kokum) juice.
Sprinkle well with wheat flour.
Fry in heated oil until brown.
Add rock salt.
Sprinkle powdered cardamom and pepper.
notes: From one of the world's oldest cookbooks. Exact chapter/verse number should be confirmed against a translated edition of the Manasollasa before publishing.

name.english: Fermented Urad Dal Steamed Cakes (medieval idli)

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, Bhartur Upabhogakarana (food/enjoyment section) — iddarika

steps: Prepare a paste from rice, black gram, asafoetida and cumin.
Keep the paste standing for one or two days until it turns sour (ferments).
Place small quantities in a Pitika (steaming vessel).
Cook by steam until done.
notes: Documented ancestor of the modern idli, using a fermented rice-and-black-gram batter steamed in a mould. Method taken from the Manasollasa cooking chapter.

name.english: Stretched Wheat Flatbread Baked on a Pan

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Mandaka

steps: Wash the wheat, dry it and powder it.
Mix the powder with ghee, salt, milk and water into a dough.
Form balls in wooden utensils and coat with pure oil.
Stretch each ball gradually by hand into a thin round.
Bake on a metallic pan over a mild fire until cooked but not blackened.
notes: An early roti/rumali-style flatbread. The text says a fourfold (very thin) variety is considered best.

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Polika

steps: Prepare wheat-flour dough balls as for Mandaka.
Place the desired sweetmeat in the centre of a stretched round.
Enclose the filling and stretch neatly using a Pesini (latticed tool).
Spread on a hot plate and bake both surfaces properly.
A slightly reddish-black finish is considered best.
notes: A documented ancestor of the stuffed sweet flatbread (puran poli / obbattu).

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Purika

steps: Prepare a wheat-flour ball as described for Mandaka.
Stretch it thin using a Pesini.
Fry properly in oil.
notes: A clear 12th-century description of the puri.

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Dosaka (Bengal-gram type)

steps: Prepare a paste from bengal gram, powdered asafoetida, cumin and salt.
Smear a small quantity of oil on a hot metallic pan.
Pour the paste onto the pan and spread it uniformly.
Cook both surfaces properly.
notes: One of the earliest documented dosa-type preparations. The text also gives a black-gram (masa) version by the same method.

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Gharika

ingredients.modern_name: bengal gram or black gram flour

steps: Prepare a thick paste from gram flour, asafoetida, cumin and salt.
Shape suitably into rounds.
Make five to seven holes in each round.
Fry properly in oil.
notes: The perforated fried ring is a clear ancestor of the vada / medu vada.

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Vatika

ingredients.modern_name: bengal gram or black gram flour

steps: Prepare a paste from gram flour, sugar, cardamom and pepper.
Shape suitably into rounds.
Fry in oil.
notes: Variations: Kanjika Vatika (the fried balls soaked in thin rice gruel) and Temana (soaked in a spiced curd mixture with ginger, coriander, cumin, pepper and asafoetida) — an early dahi-vada.

name.english: Rice Pudding with Milk and Sugar

source.author: King Someshvara III (Western Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, cooking chapter — Payasa

steps: Cook good-quality rice in buffalo milk.
Add dry ginger powder, sugar and fragrant substances.
Combine into a delicious payasa.

properties.occasion: royal court cuisine; served early in the royal dining sequence

notes: The classic kheer / payasam, described here in the 12th century.

name.english: Lotus Buds Cooked in Ghee and Spices

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Nalini

steps: Boil the lotus buds in buttermilk and squeeze out the liquid.
Cook in ghee with asafoetida, black pepper, dry ginger and spices.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetiser, hot, bitter; benefits hair; treats vertigo, fainting and spleen enlargement.

notes: The buttermilk pre-boil tempers bitterness before frying — a recurring technique for flower vegetables.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Shobhanjana

ingredients.modern_name: drumstick (moringa) flowers, with tender roots and fruits

steps: Take the drumstick flowers together with their tender roots and fruits.
Cook in oil with asafoetida and salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Sweet-smelling, digestive stimulant, pungent, hot; alleviates vata and kapha; treats spleen disorders, ulcers and worms.

notes: Moringa flowers are still cooked this way in South Indian home cooking.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Amrapallavah

steps: Boil the mango sprouts and squeeze out the liquid.
Cook in ghee with asafoetida and rock salt.
Alternatively, fry in ghee with sugar, clove and ginger for a sweet version.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetiser; treats anorexia.

notes: One record with two documented variants (savoury and sweet).

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Karirakusum

steps: Dry the hibiscus flowers in the sun.
Boil them in water.
Cook in oil with asafoetida, salt and gram flour.
Finish with buttermilk or sour gruel.

properties.ayurvedic: Purgative, pungent, astringent, appetiser; alleviates kapha and pitta.

notes: Sun-drying before cooking is an authentic preservation-and-flavour step.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, fish (Matsya) preparations section

steps: Fry coriander seeds, kasamarda and asafoetida in hot oil until brown.
Add the fish pieces and cook on low fire until tender.
Add salt and buttermilk and bring to a quick boil.
Add souring powder, dry ginger and asafoetida.
Roast (finish) in ghee.
notes: The Kshemakutuhalam also names seven fish dishes (Matsya Pralehah, Matsyakhanda Pralehah, Matsyapistika, Matsya Purana, Matsya Putapaka, Matsya Mandaka, Matsyendari) — candidates for future records once their methods are sourced.

source.text: Pre-British South Indian tradition (VITALIFE 'Before British Food' compilation)
source.author: Traditional / regional
source.citation: Arisi Upma — broken-rice and millet upma before wheat semolina (rava)

ingredients.modern_name: broken rice, coarse rice, millets or cracked wheat

steps: Roast the broken rice or millet grain until fragrant.
Temper mustard seeds, urad dal, chana dal, curry leaves, ginger and cumin in sesame oil or ghee.
Add water and bring to a boil.
Stir in the roasted grain and cook until soft.
Season with black pepper and salt.
notes: Pre-British upma used local rice and millets, not wheat semolina (rava). Rava upma spread during the WWII-era rice shortages in the Madras Presidency. Modern additions — green chilli, carrots, peas, potato, tomato, peanuts, cashews — are later. Heat traditionally came from black pepper and ginger, not chilli.

source.text: Pre-colonial South Indian tradition (VITALIFE compilation; Livemint culinary history)
source.author: Traditional / regional
source.citation: Pepper rasam before the introduction of tomato and red chilli

steps: Stone-grind the black pepper and long pepper with cumin into a coarse fresh spice mix.
Extract tamarind juice in water.
Simmer the tamarind water with the crushed pepper-spice mix, asafoetida and salt.
Temper curry leaves in sesame oil or ghee and add.
Do not add tomato or red chilli — the heat comes from pepper alone.

properties.ayurvedic: Pepper and long pepper are digestive stimulants; a traditional remedy for colds and indigestion.

notes: Pre-colonial rasam was soured with tamarind only and got its heat from black pepper and long pepper; tomato and red chilli are post-Columbian additions. Known regionally as saar, saaru, chaaru and pulusu.

name.english: Pre-Colonial Vegetable Rice (native gourds, before potato)

source.text: Pre-colonial Indian tradition (VITALIFE compilation; cf. Manasollasa rice-and-vegetable preparations)
source.author: Traditional / regional
source.period: Pre-16th century (before the potato reached India)
source.citation: Tahiri made with indigenous gourds and yam before the potato became the bulk vegetable

ingredients.modern_name: ash gourd (or native gourds, brinjal, yam)

steps: Cut the ash gourd or other native vegetables (yam, brinjal, gourds) into pieces.
Cook the rice together with the vegetables in water.
Use sesame oil or ghee as the cooking fat.
Season with black pepper and ginger; sour lightly with tamarind if desired.

properties.ayurvedic: Lighter than the modern potato version — higher water content, lower starch, more fibre.

notes: The pre-colonial tahiri used indigenous gourds and yam; the potato (an American import, post-16th century) later became the standard bulk vegetable of the modern aloo tahari. The Manasollasa describes many rice-and-vegetable dishes using indigenous vegetables.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Nispava

steps: Cut the seed vessels of the flat bean.
Cook in oil with asafoetida and salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold, heavy, strength-promoting; aggravates kapha; alleviates vata and pitta.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Brhat Patolaka

steps: Remove the vessels and cut into pieces.
Cook in ghee with asafoetida.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetiser, strength-promoting and wholesome; alleviates pitta and vata.

name.english: Sweet Bottle Gourd in Ghee and Curd

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Alabu (sweet variety)

steps: Cut into small pieces.
Cook in ghee with cumin seeds, curd and rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Cardiac tonic, heavy, appetiser and nourishing; alleviates pitta.

notes: Use only the sweet (non-bitter) bottle gourd.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Tindisaka

steps: Remove the seeds and cut into pieces.
Cook in ghee or oil with asafoetida.
Stir with a spoon until it becomes round.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetiser, cold, cardiac tonic and diuretic; alleviates pitta and kapha, aggravates vata; cures stone.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Tenti

steps: Boil the tender fruits in a small amount of water.
Cook in ghee or oil with asafoetida and spices.
Add cow's buttermilk.

properties.ayurvedic: Nourishing, appetiser, light and digestive stimulant; cures piles, worms and gulma.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Kantakari

steps: Boil the fruits in a small amount of water and cut into pieces.
Cook in ghee on a low fire.
Add rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Light, hot, digestive stimulant, pungent and bitter; alleviates vata and kapha; cures fever, cough and asthma.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Karkotaka

steps: Slit the fruits halfway and stuff with black pepper.
Cook in oil with rock salt.
Add asafoetida water.
Cook on a low fire.

properties.ayurvedic: Purgative, appetiser and digestive stimulant; cures skin disease and anorexia.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Visanaphala

steps: Cut the fruits into two pieces.
Fry in ghee with asafoetida.
Add rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold, appetiser, strength-promoting and light; alleviates pitta; cures poisoning.

name.english: Cluster Fig in Sour Buttermilk and Ghee

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Udumbara

steps: Boil the fruits in sour buttermilk.
Cook in ghee with spices and rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold, astringent and sweet, constipative; cures raktapitta and retention of urine.

name.english: Velvet Bean in Ghee and Spices

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Kapikacchu

steps: Boil the fruits.
Cook in ghee with asafoetida and spices.
Add rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Sweet, cold, heavy and unctuous; promotes strength; alleviates vata; cures ulcer.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Harita Canaka

steps: Crush the green bengal grams and wash them.
Cook in oil with asafoetida, salt and black pepper.

properties.ayurvedic: Digestive stimulant and laxative; promotes kapha; aggravates vata slightly.

notes: A ghee version cooks them with dry ginger, black pepper and asafoetida.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Phala-saka (fruit-vegetables) section — Rajamasa

steps: Cook in ghee with spices.
The tender leaves are also cooked in a similar way.

properties.ayurvedic: Cardiac tonic; alleviates kapha and pitta; produces flatulence; constipative.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Kutajapuspa

steps: Boil the flowers in sweet gruel for about two hours and squeeze out the liquid.
Cook in oil with asafoetida and salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Bowel-binding, delicious, cold and light; cures heart disease, fever and raktapitta.

name.english: Agasti Flowers in Buttermilk and Ghee

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Agastikusuma

steps: Boil the flowers and tender fruits in buttermilk.
Cook in ghee with asafoetida.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold; alleviates kapha and pitta; treats fever, colds and night blindness.

name.english: Tender Neem Sprouts in Ghee and Buttermilk

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemakutuhalam, Puspa-saka (flower-vegetables) section — Nimbapallavah

steps: Cook the tender neem sprouts in ghee with rock salt, asafoetida and buttermilk.
Reduce to a syrup-like consistency.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold, light, bowel-binding and digestive stimulant; treats ulcers, vomiting, skin conditions and diabetes.

notes: A bitter medicinal preparation; the bitterness is valued in Ayurveda.

It is also cooked.
notes: Source notes it is prepared both as a rubbed/dressed preparation and cooked.

steps: Cook the leaves in ghee with asafoetida, salt and wet ginger.
Add buttermilk and cook on a low fire.

steps: Method 1: Cook in oil with rice-powder, asafoetida and wet ginger.
Method 2: Boil in sour buttermilk, then cook in ghee with asafoetida, salt and dry ginger.
Method 3: Rub the leaves, then cook in mustard oil with black pepper, rock salt, dry ginger and asafoetida.
notes: Three distinct preparations of gram-plant leaves given.

steps: Boil the pieces and squeeze out water completely.
Cook in ghee with tamarind-leaves.

properties.ayurvedic: Described in the source as light, laxative and cold.

notes: Source describes Nali as light, laxative and cold.

ingredients.modern_name: sorrel / chuka leaves and stalks (Rumex vesicarius)

steps: Cook the cukraka with stalks in sesame oil with asafoetida and rock-salt.

steps: Boil the leaves and squeeze out water.
Cook in sesame oil with asafoetida.

steps: Rub with the kasamarda (coffee senna leaves).
Cook in oil with asafoetida and buttermilk.

steps: Rub the leaves with fragrant spices.
Cook in oil with rock salt.

steps: Boil the tender leaves.
Squeeze out water.
Cook in oil with asafoetida and buttermilk.

source.text: Kṣemakutūhala (Kshemakutuhala) of Kṣemaśarman — 4th utsava (Cooking), section 'Common preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'
source.author: Kṣemaśarman (Kshemasharma)
source.citation: Kṣemaśarman, Kṣemakutūhala, 4th utsava (Pāka), 'Common preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'; critical study on wisdomlib.org

steps: Wash the rice and soak it in buttermilk.
Boil water in a vessel.
Add the soaked rice.
When cooked, squeeze/strain out the excess water (drained-rice method).

properties.ayurvedic: Digestive stimulant, wholesome, refreshing, light and diuretic.

notes: Bhakta/Bhāta is drained boiled rice; the cooking water is discarded after the grains are done. Prepared as described on the fetched page.

source.text: Kṣemakutūhala (Kshemakutuhala) of Kṣemaśarman — 4th utsava (Cooking), section 'Common preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'
source.author: Kṣemaśarman (Kshemasharma)
source.citation: Kṣemaśarman, Kṣemakutūhala, 4th utsava (Pāka), 'Common preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'; critical study on wisdomlib.org

steps: Take an eighth part of rice and a twelfth part of halves of mudga (split green gram) pulse.
Cook them together in water.
Add saffron, turmeric powder and salt.
Ghee is added before eating.

properties.ayurvedic: Heavy, strength-promoting, nourishing and purgative; produces vata, pitta, mala and flatulence.

notes: Proportions given as fractional parts of rice to mudga pulse. Ghee is mixed in at the time of serving.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Stew the meat in plain water or in water mixed with spices.
Then fry it properly.
notes: A basic stew-then-fry method.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Remove bones and cut the meat into small pieces.
Mix the meat pieces with water, asafoetida, cumin seeds, turmeric, wet ginger, dry ginger, rock salt, black pepper, powdered rice, lemon juice, wheat flour and ghee.
Boil until it is cooked.
notes: A thick meat-and-grain porridge, related to the harisa/haleem family.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Boil the meat in a decoction of asafoetida and coriander seeds.
Crush it.
Fry asafoetida in heated ghee and add the crushed meat, cumin seeds, wet ginger, citron juice, cardamom and rock salt.
notes: A meat stuffing used inside samosas and other filled preparations.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Roll out dough into a broad strip.
Put the mutton stuffing on it.
Fold and deep fry in ghee.
notes: A meat samosa; uses the Purana mutton stuffing.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Steam the meat in water.
Thrust the spit into the pieces of meat.
Apply a paste made of curd, wet ginger, asafoetida and salt onto the pieces.
Roast on the fire.
notes: Curd-marinated spit-roast, an antecedent of kebab/tikka.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Boil the liver.
Mix the boiled liver with curd and fry with heated ghee.
Mix in curd, rock salt, asafoetida, cardamom, black pepper and wet ginger in proper quantity.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Light the charcoal in a big hollow (pit oven).
Hang the meat in it.
When it is baked, it is called Tandura.
notes: Cooking in a charcoal-fired pit oven (tandoor).

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Cut the meat into pieces and mix with spices.
Wrap up in leaves and shape into a round.
Roast in the fire.
notes: A leaf-wrapped roasting method (puta cooking).

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Put pieces of meat inside a fruit.
Cook it as in the putapaka method (roasted in fire).
notes: A variant of putapaka using a fruit as the casing instead of leaves.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Mix the meat with spices and form small and big rounds.
Steam them and then fry in ghee.
Dip them in spicy buttermilk or curry.

properties.ayurvedic: Said to be an alleviator of vata and a promoter of strength; beneficial to a wounded person and to one having semen in very small quantity

notes: Classed among the Praleha meat preparations.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Stuff a cake of masura (lentil) pulse with the meat and shape into balls.
Wrap up in leaves and boil them.
Mix in powdered black pepper, oil or ghee and salt.
Cook well.
Fumigate with perfumed smoke.
notes: Meat encased in lentil cake, boiled and finished with aromatic fumigation.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda (recipe attributed to Kashyapa-samhita); English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Cook the meat in ghee and water.
Mix in powdered dry ginger, milk and sugar.
Add sweet-smelling spices and make it semi-liquid.
notes: A sweet, semi-liquid meat dish attributed to the Kashyapa-samhita.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Roast the head of the animal on strong fire.
Wash it well and rub to remove the hair.
Cut it into pieces and cook them in ghee or oil with salt and spices.
notes: Preparation of the animal's head, akin to modern 'siri' dishes.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Wash and clean the intestines.
Steam them in a decoction of asafoetida.
Cut into pieces and mix with spices.
Fry them in oil or ghee.
notes: Offal/intestine preparation.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Boil the meat in buttermilk.
Deep fry it in ghee.
Mix in black mustard powder, rock salt, spices and curd.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Slit the brinjals halfway.
Stuff them with meat that has been prepared by the putapaka method.
notes: Stuffed eggplant using putapaka-cooked meat as the filling.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Remove the wings and rub the meat with citron juice, wet ginger and rock salt.
Mix in cardamom and cloves.
Crush and shape into balls.
Steam the balls for a while.
Cut them and roast on an iron spit.
notes: A bird (poultry/game) preparation.

source.author: Kshemasharma
source.citation: Kshemasharma, Kshemakutuhala — Cooking rules and usage of Meat in Ayurveda; English critical study, wisdomlib.org

steps: Remove the wings and skin of the birds and boil the meat.
Roast it on an iron spit.
Mix in salt and spices.
Deep fry in oil or ghee.
notes: An alternative bird preparation method.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Method 1: Boil the milk and allow it to cool. Collect the cream formed on the surface. Boil the cream to obtain ghee.
Method 2: Churn the curd and collect the butter. Boil it and prepare ghee.

properties.ayurvedic: Rejuvenating, cold; alleviates pitta and vata. Cow's ghee aids digestion and eyesight; buffalo's ghee is aphrodisiac; goat's ghee helps asthma and cough.

notes: Two preparation methods given (cream-boiling and butter-boiling).

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Add one-fourth quantity of water to thick curd.
Churn the mixture.
Strain through a clean cloth.
Add fried asafoetida, cumin seeds, salt and mustard in small quantity.

properties.ayurvedic: Considered to be an ambrosia (amrita) for human beings.

notes: The text describes five varieties of takra including Ghola, Hinguvasita Agholaka, Gaurita Takra and Acchika (listed as separate recipes here).

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix curd with milk and strain through a cloth.
Add asafoetida and rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Alleviates vata; nourishing, strength-promoting, an appetiser; cures piles.

notes: A variety of takra (buttermilk) blended with milk.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Add dry ginger, black pepper, salt, cumin seeds and powdered orange skin to the curd.
Churn the mixture.
Add fried asafoetida.

properties.ayurvedic: An appetiser and carminative.

notes: A spiced variety of takra.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Strain takra prepared two to three days before through a cloth.
Mix in rock salt.
Fumigate with fragrant smoke.

properties.ayurvedic: Exceedingly appetising.

notes: Uses buttermilk aged two to three days.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Boil the milk and allow it to cool.
Mix in a small quantity of buttermilk and keep it in a fresh vessel.
After a few hours the curd is ready.
Serve taken with cumin seeds, rock salt and wet ginger.

properties.ayurvedic: Stimulates digestion; alleviates vata and kapha. Cow's curd is a digestive stimulant and nourishing.
properties.season: Best in winter and the rainy season; not to be taken at night; avoided in summer, autumn and spring.

notes: Rules of taking curd are given: not eaten at night; avoided in summer, autumn and spring; ideally consumed in winter and rainy seasons.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Boil curdled milk in a broad vessel and stir continuously until a thick residue is left.
Tie it in a cloth and allow the liquid to drain out.
Cook until only the powder is left.
Rub it through a strainer.
notes: A milk-solids powder made from curdled milk.

name.english: Fried chhena dumplings in milk or syrup

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Shape curdled milk into vataka and vati (dumplings/patties).
Fry them in ghee.
Drop the fried pieces into milk or sugar syrup.
notes: The critical study relates this to the Bengali sweet 'Rasagulla'.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Crush curdled milk and rice paste together.
Form rounds and fry them in ghee.
Mix with sugar syrup and shape into balls.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix curdled milk and sugar.
Churn the mixture.
Cook on a low fire until only the powder is left.

name.english: Milk-solids with parched rice and almond

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix curdled milk with laja (fried rice), grapes, sugar and the pulp of fresh cuddapah almond.
Cook on a low fire and prepare Tilavana.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Cook the paste of wheat flour in ghee.
Make rounds with a hollow interior.
Fill the milk paste into the hollow and seal.
Fry in ghee.
notes: Name reconstructed from the printed heading 'KRS ARAGAR BHAKA'; a stuffed milk dumpling.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Cut the curdled milk into pieces and deep-fry in ghee.
Cook the fried pieces with spices.
notes: A savoury spiced paneer-style preparation.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Fry the refined wheat flour in a small quantity of ghee.
Keep adding milk continuously and cook on a low fire.
When cooked, add one-fourth part of sugar.
Cook until the ghee separates and is seen.
Add clove and black pepper.
notes: Refined wheat flour is documented here in the historical source. A lapsi/halwa-type preparation.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Knead the refined wheat flour with milk.
Add sugar, camphor and black pepper.
Form rounds and deep-fry in ghee.

properties.ayurvedic: Heavy; a cardiac tonic and appetiser; promotes strength and semen; alleviates pitta and vata.

notes: Also called Ghevara (modern Ghevar). Refined wheat flour documented in the historical source.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix refined wheat flour with coconut, sugar and wet ginger.
Knead it with the pulp of coconut milk.
Shape the rounds and deep-fry in ghee.
notes: A coconut variety of Ghevara. Refined wheat flour documented in the historical source.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix refined wheat flour with curdled milk and sugar.
Form rounds.
Shallow-fry in ghee.
notes: A curdled-milk variety of Ghevara.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix water chestnut powder with milk and sugar.
Form rounds.
Shallow-fry in ghee.
notes: A water-chestnut variety of Ghevara.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Boil the rice flour in milk.
Add sugar.
Form rounds and fry in ghee.
notes: A rice-flour variety of Ghevara.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Fry the juice of mango in ghee and mix in sugar.
Shape into balls.
Shallow-fry in ghee.
notes: A mango variety of Ghevara.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Mix one-eighth part of fresh barnyard millet with whole milk and cook it.
Add ghee and sugar.

properties.ayurvedic: Heavy, constipative (binding); cures vata, raktapitta and burning sensation.

notes: A payasa made with barnyard millet (syamaka) rather than rice.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Shallow-fry the pulp of naranga (orange).
Add ghee and sugar.
Allow it to cool.
Mix in half-boiled milk in proper quantity.
Perfume it with fragrant spices.

properties.ayurvedic: Heavy, constipative (binding); alleviates vata and pitta.

source.author: Kṣemaśarma (Kshemasharma); critical study and translation by Hiteshbhai Vrajalal Bhuptani
source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

steps: Cut the soft pulp of coconut into small pieces.
Boil the pieces in water.
Mix them with well-boiled milk and sugar.
Fumigate with the smoke of agaru (eaglewood).

properties.ayurvedic: Unctuous, cold, heavy, nourishing; promotes semen; alleviates pitta and vata.

source.citation: Kshemakutuhala by Kshemasharma – A Critical Study, ed. H. V. Bhuptani (1988), chapter 'Milk products and preparations in Ayurvedic cookery'

ingredients.original: boiling water (poured via a goduka vessel)

steps: To remove the hair, first cover the animal with a white piece of cloth.
Slowly pour boiling water over the body of the boar using a goduka (a handled vessel for drawing water from a large earthen pot) until the hair is loosened from the roots and can be removed by hand.
Alternatively, besmear the boar with mud and burn the skin with a fire made of grass.
Cook the meat over a mild (low) fire, which the text recommends as best for meat-food, so that the meat shrinks little, stays juicier and is more delicious.

properties.occasion: Royal court cuisine (annabhoga / mamsavarga meat cookery)

notes: The fetched page details the dehairing/cleaning of the boar and the general principle of cooking meat on a mild fire, rather than a full spiced dish with quantities. Only what is present in the fetched text is recorded here.

steps: Sour juice was added to milk (to curdle it).
The liquid part of the whey was strained through a cloth.
With this strained whey liquid was mixed some juice of ripe tamarind fruit.

properties.occasion: A sweet drink (panaka) taken by the king between courses during meals

notes: Attributed specifically to the Manasollasa on the fetched page. The same page attributes other fruit-based cold drinks (from jujube, myrobalan, pomegranate, tamarind, citron) to the Lokopakara, not the Manasollasa, so those are excluded. Ingredient quantities are not given in the source.

source.text: Pākadarpaṇam (Pakadarpana) of King Nala — non-vegetarian rice preparation, as described in the book review of 'The Pākadarpaṇam: The text on Indian cookery by King Nala'

source.citation: Book Review, 'The Pāka darpaṇam: The text on Indian cookery by King Nala', Ancient Science of Life, Apr-Jun 2014, Vol. 33, Issue 4, pp. 259-260

region: Ancient/medieval India (Nishadha kingdom; Sanskrit Pākaśāstra tradition)

ingredients.modern_name: meat (boiled or unboiled), cut into pieces the size of rice grains

ingredients.quantity: a little, plus freshly prepared ghee for seasoning

steps: Take three parts of water and one part of rice and put to boil.
When the rice begins to boil, add meat (boiled or unboiled) cut into small pieces the size of the rice grains, along with a little rock salt.
Mix well and add a little quantity of ghee.
When the water is dried up, take the vessel out of the fire.
Season the preparation with coconut milk and freshly prepared ghee, along with attractive flowers of ketakī (Pandanus fascicularis) and pieces of parpaṭa.
Give it its unique fragrance using camphor and musk.
Close the vessel with the upper lid, keep it on the fire and mix well.
When the dish becomes soft, serve it for eating.

properties.ayurvedic: Described as tasty, aphrodisiac, wholesome and light for digestion; gives strength to the body, nourishes all the tissues, and heals wounds.

notes: The source names further specific non-vegetarian rice variants of this preparation — mudga taṇḍula māṃsānna (green-gram meat rice), plāvaka māṃsodana (sparrow-meat biriyani), and kukkuṭa māṃsodana (chicken biriyani) — but gives no distinct ingredients or method for them, so they are not listed as separate recipes. The text also warns of 'gara viṣa' (combinatorial poison), e.g. sesame oil plus camphor, noting such combinations become non-toxic when used with meat and cooked rice.

ingredients.original: ārdraka (ginger, for medicated water and pieces)

ingredients.modern_name: Coriander (Coriandrum sativum), seed powder and spice

steps: Take a lovely young brinjal fruit and cut off its upper portion with a sharp-edged knife.
Cut the brinjal into two parts and drop it into a pot filled with water so the round fruit is cleansed.
Dip it into water medicated with ginger.
Mix it with asafoetida, Kaayaphala (Kaidarya / curry leaf) and coriander powder.
Add pieces of garlic and ginger and keep it on the fire.
Cut the round brinjal fruit into pieces and keep them in hot water for a while, then bring them out of the water.
Make a paste of spices — black pepper, coriander and cumin seeds (jeera) — mixed with ripe tamarind and curd.
Coat the brinjal pieces with this paste and fry them in cow's ghee (clarified butter).
Take the pieces out and make them fragrant with camphor.

properties.ayurvedic: Praised in the text as an alleviator of Tridosha (balances all three doshas) and an enhancer of strength

notes: Only concrete vegetable recipe reproduced verbatim on the fetched source page. Original Sanskrit dish-name is not given on the page (it presents the dish in English as a 'brinzal/brinjal' preparation); 'Vārtāka śāka' is supplied as the standard Sanskrit term for a brinjal vegetable dish. The page glosses Kaayaphala as 'Kaidarya', which in the same tradition's translations denotes curry leaf (Murraya koenigii). Ingredient Sanskrit names in 'original' beyond those explicitly on the page are the conventional Sanskrit equivalents of the English ingredient words quoted; no quantities are specified in the source.

steps: Take fruits such as mango and remove their seeds/stones, keeping them separate.
Mix the fruit and heat it together with sugar.
When the mixture becomes semi-solid, add a little water.
Filter the mixture through a clean cloth with minute holes.
Season the lehya with fragrant flowers.

properties.ayurvedic: Lehya is one of the five intake categories (lickables) in the text; prescribed to be seasoned with fragrant flowers.

notes: From Chapter 8 (Lehya Prakaranam, 9 verses), which covers sauce-like lickable dishes made from fruits like mango. The text states 'all lehyas such as the one prepared out of mango' follow this method. Source consulted is a scholarly book review summarizing the translated text.

Pass the water through sand.
Treat the water with fragrant flowers.

steps: Fry asafoetida and turmeric in ghee or oil.
Wash the finely cut boneless pieces of mutton or other meat and cook them slowly in this ghee.
Add an appropriate amount of water and salt to it.
When the meat pieces are cooked well, add the vesavara (masala) to it.
Prepare the vesavara by mixing powders of betel leaves, rice grains, cloves and black pepper in a particular proportion.
notes: Base plain-meat preparation; the vesavara is the flavouring masala. Serves as the foundation for other meat dishes such as mamsashringataka.

steps: Make long thin threads from samita.
Dry them in the sun.
Cook them in milk and savour after adding ghee.
notes: Described as very similar to vermicelli kheer (payasam).

steps: Make long, thin pieces from samita kneaded with ghee.
Place these pieces side by side on a wooden slab.
Knead them all together with a kneading device so that a single rounded disc is formed.
Cut this disc with a knife such that the pieces remain together.
Knead the cut pieces again and smear them with the shakata mixture.
Mix each piece together to make a ball; spread these balls so that a spherical disc is formed.
Fry this circular disc in ghee so that it develops multiple layers.
Finally sprinkle sugar mixed with fragrant ingredients over it.
notes: Layered flaky sweet; source notes variants made with wheat flour (godhuma-phenika) or black gram flour (masha-phenika).

steps: Mix one adhaka of sour curd derived from buffalo milk with two prasthas of sugar.
Allow this solution to filter into a vessel through a cloth.
Add powdered cardamom, cloves, camphor and black pepper to the resultant liquid.
notes: The page details generic shikharini recipes; Raghunatha also names a variety called sushena-shikharini (recorded separately).

Make the mixture in the shape of vatas.
Fry these vatas in ghee till the water content is fully evaporated.
Immerse these vatas in sugar syrup dressed with cardamom, cloves, camphor and black pepper.
notes: Source compares this preparation to badusha (balushahi), a famous sweet.

steps: Hold sweet lime, wood-apple, wood sorrel, tamarind, gooseberry and pomegranate together with sugar and mustard in a clean piece of cloth.
Prepare a rasala using dry ginger, pepper, cumin seeds, cardamom (caturjataka) and the spreading grass bhustrna along with wet ginger.
Add this rasala skilfully to the fruit mixture.
Collect the liquid flowing through the cloth.
notes: The same source page also gives a second sushena-shikharini variant: mix ghee, jaggery, cumin seeds, dry ginger, wet ginger and powdered cardamom (caturjataka) together and put the mixture into curd.

Fry the samita balls in ghee.

Cook them in ghee.
Then immerse them in sugar syrup.
notes: Known as shankhapala; comparable to the modern shankarpali when made without syrup.

Mix the fried vermicelli with sugar syrup and prepare laddus.

steps: Combine dried ginger, black pepper, long pepper, nut grass rhizomes, cinnamon, cinnamon leaves, cardamom, catechu, coriander and honey in equal proportion.
To use, add the mixture to water and rinse the mouth to obtain good mouth odour.

properties.ayurvedic: Thick gruel abounding in grain shreds; heavier than Peya and Manda.

notes: Fetched text: 'A gruel, which abounds with such seedy shreds, is called Vilepi.' No numeric ratio given in fetched text.

Fry the pulse, then cook it into a soup (Yusha).

properties.ayurvedic: Light pulse broth.

properties.ayurvedic: Roasted spiced meat.

Make it into a dough with water, of a consistency that is neither too thick nor too thin.

properties.ayurvedic: Barley-flour preparation.

notes: Fetched text: 'Powdered barley soaked in clarified butter and made into a dough with water, which is neither too thick nor too thin.'

source.author: King Someshvara III (Bhulokamalla), Kalyani Chalukya dynasty
source.citation: Manasollasa 5.10.431-449 (recipes for various kinds of wine); Sanskrit verse: 'gudaiksurasasambhutam kalena vikrtim gatam | dhataki-puspasamsiktam khamdasammisritam madhu'

region: Deccan / Karnataka (Kalyani Chalukya kingdom), South India
steps: Take sugarcane juice or jaggery as the base.
Allow it to transform (ferment) over time.
Infuse/sprinkle it with dhataki flowers (a traditional fermentation agent).
Mix in khanda (sugar) to finish the wine.

properties.ayurvedic: Described as having katu-tikta rasa (pungent-bitter taste); intoxicating, with several varieties
properties.occasion: Wine drinking permitted, especially on festival occasions; no general prohibition stated

notes: The wisdomlib essay states 'Recipes for various kinds of wine are given in the Manasollasa (5.10.431-449)'. The verbatim Sanskrit verse describes madhu produced from sugarcane juice/jaggery, aged over time, infused with dhataki flowers and mixed with sugar. Only this fragment is reproduced on the fetched page.

name.english: Fermented liquors (palm, coconut, date, grape, sugarcane)

source.text: Manasollasa — art of preparing wine and asava
source.author: King Someshvara III (Bhulokamalla), Kalyani Chalukya dynasty
source.citation: Manasollasa, chapter on brewing alcoholic beverages (Talimadya, Narikelasava, Khajurasava, and grape/sugarcane wine); as summarised on Wikipedia's Manasollasa article

region: Deccan / Karnataka (Kalyani Chalukya kingdom), South India
steps: Select the fermentable base: grape or sugarcane for the common wines; or unusual sources — palm sap (Talimadya), coconut (Narikelasava), or date (Khajurasava).
Brew/ferment the juice or sap of the chosen base to produce the asava.

properties.occasion: Manufacture and consumption of liquor permitted, notably on festival occasions

notes: The fetched Wikipedia page names these asava/wine types and their base ingredients but does not reproduce full step-by-step methods; the method here is the implied brewing/fermentation of each named base. Detailed verse-level recipes are said to lie in Manasollasa 5.10.431-449.

name.english: Chicken simmered in sour ajika water with ginger, fenugreek and coriander, finished with ghee, garlic and asafoetida

source.text: Manasollasa (Abhilashitartha Chintamani) of King Someshvara III, 12th century CE — meat (mamsa) preparations of the annabhoga section; translated and reconstructed on the 'Manasollasa Dishes' page.
source.author: King Someshvara III (Western/Kalyani Chalukya dynasty)
source.citation: Manasollasa, annabhoga (meat) section; Irayari Vairavi, 'Manasollasa Dishes' (fetched 2026-07-31).

ingredients.quantity: 2 lbs white meat (modern reconstruction; not specified in original)

ingredients.modern_name: sour fermented rice gruel / kanji (souring liquid)

steps: Cut the meat into pieces the size of an amla (Indian gooseberry) fruit.
Place the pieces in ajika water together with adraka (ginger) and boil.
Then add sothi, sour substances, salt, powder of methi (fenugreek) and dhanyaka (coriander), and green dhanyaka (fresh coriander); cook well.
Remove from the fire and 'mend' (finish) it by adding ghee, garlic and hingu (asafoetida).
Close with a lid.
notes: Original method text quoted verbatim from the fetched page; the page also gives a modern reconstruction with measured quantities, noted here as reconstruction, not original. 'Ajika' denotes a sour/fermented liquid; 'sothi' and 'sour substances' are souring agents in the translation.

region: Deccan / Tanjavur Maratha court, medieval India

ingredients.modern_name: alkali salt (translated 'nitrate of potash'; a soda/nitre leavening-alkali)

steps: Soak split black gram in water and remove its outer skin.
Dry it in the sun and powder it; this flour is called dhumasi.
Mix the flour with asafoetida, turmeric, salt, cumin seeds and svarjikakshara (nitrate of potash).
Knead the mixture and spread it out as thin slices.
Cook the slices either by heating them directly in the embers or by frying them in oil.
notes: svarjikakshara is rendered in the translation as 'nitrate of potash'; it is an alkaline leavening/curing salt. The skinned-and-powdered black-gram flour is specifically named dhumasi.

source.author: Raghunatha Suri (Raghunatha Ganesha Navahasta)
source.citation: Bhojanakutuhala of Raghunatha Suri, Siddhannaprakarana (section devoted to vatakas); reproduced on the Wisdomlib entry for Vataka (from the Shodhganga thesis on Bhojanakutuhala).

region: Deccan / Tanjavur Maratha court, medieval India
steps: Prepare the vataka batter chiefly from black gram, mixing in constituents such as ginger and asafoetida (which aid digestion of the black gram).
Cook the vatakas by one of several methods: some are fried in gingelly oil, some in ghee, some are dried in the sun and then fried in oil, while others are immersed in liquids.

properties.ayurvedic: The ginger and asafoetida are said to help proper digestion of the black gram.

notes: The Bhojanakutuhala devotes a whole section to vatakas; most are made of black gram. The author Sanskritizes Marathi 'vate' as 'vataka' and 'vati' as 'vatika'. Named varieties elsewhere in the text include surana-vataka.

source.author: Raghunatha Suri (Raghunatha Ganesha Navahasta)

region: Deccan / Tanjavur Maratha court, medieval India
steps: Make thin cakes from dry wheat flour.
Cook them in a pan so as to form thin slices.
Heat the slices directly in the fire.
notes: The text says rotika can also be made using barley flour, black-gram flour, split black-gram flour or Bengal-gram (chickpea) flour instead of wheat.

name.english: Ghee-fried wheat rounds filled with milk paste

Make rounds with a hollow interior.
Fill the milk paste into the hollow and seal.
Fry in ghee.

Form rounds.
Pour sugar syrup over the rounds.

Cook them with spices.
notes: A savory paneer-like preparation.

steps: Shallow fry the pulp of naranga (orange).
Add ghee and sugar and allow it to cool.
Mix in half-boiled milk in proper quantity.
Perfume with fragrant spices.

steps: Mix mango juice with sugar, cardamom, clove and ginger root.

properties.ayurvedic: Delicious, heavy, cardiac tonic and appetiser.

Add water, sugar, cardamom and juice of wet ginger.

properties.ayurvedic: Heavy; cardiac tonic; promotes semen.

Mix sugar, cardamom, black pepper, fresh ghee and thin cream.
Prepare it in syrup form.

notes: Two variant methods given.

steps: Mix refined wheat flour with sugar and water into a thick paste.
Deep fry in ghee.
notes: Apupa is an ancient Indian fried sweet cake, attested since Vedic times.

Mix with milk to make a thick paste.
Pour the thick paste through a coconut-shell cup with a hole at the bottom, in a whirling manner, over hot ghee.
Fry, then drop into sugar syrup.
notes: Identified in the source with jalebi.

Fill them with processed sugar, camphor and ghee and seal the ends.
Deep fry in ghee.

steps: Stew the meat in the decoction of alkaline herbs (kutheraka, prthu, gunja, apamarga).
Cook by the general method.
Add perfumed sprinkles.

properties.ayurvedic: Appetizer; promotes strength and semen; digestive stimulant.

notes: Meat cooked in an alkaline-herb decoction and perfumed.

steps: Cut the meat into big pieces and wash them.
Heat oil or ghee and put in the pieces; stir constantly.
When cooked, add water and salt; boil till bubbling.
Add pomegranate juice in big quantity.
When cooked properly, add cumin seeds and dry ginger.
Separate the pieces of meat from the Praleha and strain through a cloth.
Fumigate it with the smoke of ghee and asafoetida.

properties.ayurvedic: Strength-promoting; alleviates vata and pitta (varies by meat type).

notes: Praleha comes in nine named colour/type varieties (Gaura, Pattala, Dhananjaya, Gaudadesiya, Purana, Shuklavarna, Pittavarna, Haritavarna, Raktavarna).

Boil the meat first.
Cook it in ghee with asafoetida, rock salt and spices.

properties.ayurvedic: Promotes muscle tissue; alleviates vata and pitta.

notes: Species-specific preparation for castrated goat.

Fry them in ghee or oil.
Add cumin seeds, rock salt and pomegranate juice.
Cook till it becomes syrupy.

properties.ayurvedic: Cold; appetizer; light; alleviates all doshas.

notes: Venison preparation.

Cook it in oil with asafoetida and rock salt.

properties.ayurvedic: Heavy, hot, unctuous, aphrodisiac; causes burning sensation and constipation.

source.author: Kshemasharma (Kshemasharman)

Boil the pieces, then wash again with water and buttermilk.
Add spices and sour juices.
Then make into a Praleha, or fry it.

properties.ayurvedic: Alleviates vata and pitta; promotes strength.

source.author: Kshemasharma (Kshemasharman)

Remove the meat from the skull and cut into pieces.
Cook the pieces in mustard oil with asafoetida, rock salt and spices.
Add pomegranate juice.

properties.ayurvedic: Promotes strength and semen; hot, unctuous, laxative.

steps: Cook the meat of the peacock in ghee with spices.
Add rock salt, black pepper and cardamom.

properties.ayurvedic: Hot, heavy, astringent; alleviates vata and kapha.
properties.season: Should be avoided in the rainy season (as the bird then eats insects and snakes).

notes: Historical preparation; peacock is legally protected today.

Having mixed together roasted and peeled sesame seeds, potherbs, camphor, musk, cardamoms and cloves, put them into the puri.

name.english: Rice Fried in Ghee with Camphor and Ambergris

When it becomes hot, flavour it with camphor, rosewater and white ambergris.
Then, having mixed rice with saffron and salt, put it in the ghee and fry it well.
notes: An aromatic fried-rice preparation; a precursor to the saffron pulao tradition.

name.english: Qaliya of Meat, Milk and Rice

When it has become well-flavoured, put the meat, mixed with chopped potherbs, into the ghee.
When it has become marinated, add water and add, to an equal amount, one sir of cow's milk.
When it has come to the boil, add the washed rice.
notes: A qaliya-style meat dish cooked together with rice in milk.

By the same method, make chickpea-pulse phini.

steps: Take grated coconut powder, mix it with jaggery or sugar and grind it.
Mix in cardamom powder and edible camphor powder.
Put this mixture into stretched wheat flour balls, flatten them and bake them.
For an alternate filling, mix dry grapes, dates or ripened jackfruit pieces with boiled milk, parched gingelly (sesame) seeds, sugar and ghee, and grind them.
Stuff each portion into stretched wheat balls, flatten them and bake them.

properties.ayurvedic: Described among the light, palatable soups in the Kritanna section (to be taken on a physician's advice).

notes: Kambalika is a sour soup made from curd-cream and pomegranate juice. The fetched text gives only these two core components.

steps: Make vada (fritters) from Bengal-gram flour (besan) and fry them.
Immerse the fried besan vada into 'kadhi' (kwathita) made from kokum, curd and gram flour.

properties.ayurvedic: Nourishing meat broth (part of the prepared-food/kritanna class)

ingredients.modern_name: mung dal, urad dal, or chana dal (split, hulled)

steps: Cook mung dal, urad dal or chana dal in water until it reaches the consistency of gruel.
Grind cardamom, cumin, coriander, black pepper and mustard seeds into a paste and stir into the cooked dal.
Flavor the mixture with souring agents such as tamarind and lemon juice.
Garnish with mustard seeds, cumin seeds, asafoetida and curry leaves fried in a small quantity of ghee or oil.
notes: Served over cooked rice. The final tempering of spices fried in ghee/oil is an ancient technique still in use; red chilli pepper was only added to such spice mixes after the sixteenth century.

steps: Cook the bitter melon leaves, tamarind shoots, castor shoots and Palasha flowers separately in lime water.
Wash them in cold water.
Prepare any vegetable dish (palya) with them as desired.
notes: The lime-water blanch removes bitterness/acridity before the greens are seasoned. Each item is cooked separately.

steps: Soak the shoots of pipal tree in buttermilk.
Add tender leaves of bael fruit and salt.
Add water, milk, Indian gooseberry and mango, and cook.
The final product will be a soft and savory dish.

name.english: Coral-berry leaf and red-hibiscus coral dish

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

ingredients.modern_name: leaves of cupped coral-berry tree (Breynia retusa)

steps: Grind small cut pieces of coral-berry leaves with salt and lime juice.
Separately grind red hibiscus flowers in buttermilk.
Mix the two together.
The result is a light coral-colored savory dish.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Soak crushed thorn apple in lime water for one day.
The next day wash it in water.
Boil the washed crushed thorn apple along with leaves of jequirity, Indian white oleander, Indian lotus plant and lime water.
Roast the boiled thorn apple with ghee.
Any recipe made from this would be very delicious.

properties.ayurvedic: Elaborate lime-water soaking, boiling and roasting steps serve to detoxify an otherwise poisonous plant before eating.

notes: Thorn apple (Datura) is toxic; the multi-stage lime-water treatment described is a detoxification procedure. Not recommended to reproduce.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Soak barley in milk and dry it in the sun.
Dry-roast the dried barley and grind it into fine flour using a stone mortar.
Mix in a spice powder made of saffron, cinnamon, cinnamon leaves and cardamom.
Mix with sugar and ghee to make a tasty and nutritious dish.

properties.ayurvedic: Described as a nutritious dish.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Soak cleaned barley in hot milk and grind it into a paste.
Shape the paste into small balls.
Fry the balls in ghee.
This dish is called ghrta pureta.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Mix wheat flour with water to make a dough.
Soak the dough in a mixture of hot milk and ghee.
Powder cardamom, cinnamon, saffron, cinnamon leaves and sugar and mix with tender coconut water.
Add this spiced water to the dough and knead.
Place it in an urn and seal the urn with a thick mud coating.
Place the closed urn in the middle of hot embers in a wood-burning stove.
When fully cooked, take it out. This dish is called Khandaghrta pura in Kannada.
notes: An early ember/urn-baking technique for a spiced wheat sweet.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Add yogurt culture to boiled milk and allow it to ferment.
Add hot ghee to it and stir well.
Stir in hand-pounded brown rice flour and cook until it has a dough-like consistency.
Using a hand press, make fine thin noodles with this dough.
Make sugar syrup and stir in milk and the noodles.
Shape it into small balls.
notes: An early form of savige/sevai (rice vermicelli). Variations and adaptations remain popular across South India.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

ingredients.modern_name: dates, grapes, or jujube fruit pulp (finely chopped)

steps: Make a dough with rice flour, fermented milk and ghee (as in the savige recipe).
Roll it out into thin flat breads and cook them on a griddle.
Pound the flat breads into a fine powder.
Mix finely chopped dates, grapes or jujube-fruit pulp into this powder.
Add the required quantity of sugar syrup and knead into a dough.
Add powder of saffron, cinnamon, cinnamon leaves and edible camphor and knead again.
Shape the dough into small balls. It is called khanda ladduge.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Smear the inside of a clay pot with mango juice.
Add hot milk to the pot.
When it ferments, the yogurt will have the fragrance of mango.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

ingredients.modern_name: powder of Indian mallow (Abutilon indicum) or country mallow (Sida cordifolia)

steps: Reduce buffalo milk to half its quantity by boiling.
Stir in powders of Indian mallow or country mallow.
Add ghee, sugar, and powders of cinnamon, cinnamon leaves and cardamom to this hot liquid and mix well.
The milk will coagulate.
Make balls with the coagulated milk.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

ingredients.modern_name: shoots of jambul (Eugenia jambolana / Syzygium cumini)

steps: Combine jackfruit pods, edible camphor, sesame oil and shoots of jambul.
Keep the mixture in sunlight to extract the juice.
notes: One of several sun-driven juice-extraction techniques.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

steps: Smear the rose apple fruits with sugarcane juice.
Keep them in sunlight to draw out the juice.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

ingredients.modern_name: tender leaves of Bermuda grass or rose apple leaves

steps: Grind together tamarind flowers, chitraka root, black pepper, tender banana, and tender leaves of Bermuda grass or rose apple leaves.
Mix with the pulp of ripe bananas.
Keep it in sunlight.

source.author: Chavundaraya II
source.citation: Lokopakara of Chavundaraya II (1025 CE), Chapter VIII 'Supa sastra' (cookery); English translation/adaptation by Ammini Ramachandran, 'Lokopakara – Part III Recipes', Peppertrail (2012).

ingredients.modern_name: Samarang rose apple (Myrtus samarangense / Syzygium samarangense)

steps: Smear the Samarang rose apple with a mixture of borax, edible camphor, thorn apple seeds and common jasmine leaves.
Keep it in sunlight; the fruit will exude its juice.
notes: Contains thorn-apple (Datura) seeds, which are toxic; not recommended to reproduce.
